newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Ex-Sweden air cargo rates to Far East edge higher.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Sweden air cargo rates to Far East edge higher.

text.p: A wave of price increases pushed some ex-Sweden air cargo rates higher, but some market players surveyed by Reuters said factors like the fuel surcharge could stop price rises from sticking.
"I think if this situation continues there will be decreases in rates. People are asking for lower rates," said Karl Berg, of Finnair's cargo division.
Scandinavia airline SAS and Lufthansa Cargo both announced cargo rate increases of between seven and 10 percent from Sweden in their summer timetables.
Sven Ahlberg, Lufthansa Cargo manager for Sweden, said the airline had enjoyed a couple busy months.
"It was a very good February. We are on top of last year's figures by about 10 percent and January and February last year were good," he said.
Anders Uddman, head of British Airways World Cargo in Sweden, also said demand had been good lately and that two important, high yielding markets were rebounding -- South America and South East Asia.
"They were very soft last year at this time," he said.
British Airways had recently moved a 32 tonne shipment of ship spares from Sweden.
"It's not that often that we get a one-off, ad hoc shipment of ship spares," Uddman said.
He said price increases were difficult to push through. "Although some airlines have talked about raising prices from April 1 we haven't seen many of them sticking," Uddman said.
Paul Rudorff, of freight forwarder Wilson, said airlines were silent on how long the fuel surcharge would last, much to the market's chagrin, but that they were strict on rate rises.
"All airlines have been asking for 10 percent more and they're pretty tough," said Rudorff.
SAS said last week it was considering ending fuel surcharges on both passenger and cargo flights after U.S. airline group Delta dropped the levy.

Forwarders said it was not a problem to find capacity to the U.S.. The rate was steady at 10 crowns per kg. To Chicago the rate was slightly higher at 11.30 compared to 11.20 crowns at the time of the last Reuters market report on January 13.
To Los Angeles it was higher at 12.90 crowns versus 12.70.

"We have strong outbound right now," said Anders Brag of American Airlines, which flies non-stop from Stockholm to Chicago. "All of our customers have had a little bit more than expected. We are considering a rate increase."

Rates to the Far East were mixed to slightly higher, the survey showed, with the average market price to Hong Kong up at 13.50 crowns compared to 13.40 and to Singapore it rose to 13.60 from 13.50 crowns. Rates to Bangkok were steady at 13.10.
The rate to Japan rose to 19.85 from 19.65 crowns.

"In the second half of February it was maybe a bit quieter than expected. We've had no especially big shipments, no extra contracts," said Peter Sull, cargo and sales manager for Scandinavia & Finland for Thai Airways.
"The Far East is fully booked every week," another freight forwarder said. "The Far East will be bigger in the coming two to three months. China and the Far East will grow too."
Bjorn Thun, of Singapore Airlines' cargo division in Sweden, said there had been some ad hoc shipments going for slightly lower rates in the slow months of January and February.
"We see much less of that now. Now the market's starting to roll again so there's no room for ad hoc shipments," Thun said.
Thun said there was lots of freight to Jakarta and Manila lately and traffic to Australia was also busy.
Singapore Airlines trucks freight from Sweden to Copenhagen to its Boeing 747 freighter which operates twice weekly.

The carrier said it planned to increase freight rates from Denmark and Norway by five to seven percent in its summer timetable but that it would leave ex-Sweden and ex-Finland rates the same in order to level prices from the Nordic region.
The average market rate to Sao Paolo in Brazil was slightly lower at 20.70 crowns per kg compared to 20.80 crowns.
To Dubai the rate was 10.00 compared to 10.20 crowns. "If you have a big shipment you can go down a little. We are shipping mostly machinery," one forwarder said.

To Johannesburg, South Africa, where the rate was lower at 20.10 crowns per kg compared to 20.30 crowns, forwarders said they were handling machinery and Ericsson telecoms. On the way back they were flying fruit, wine and flowers.
The rate to London was nearly steady at 7.45 crowns per kg compared to 7.55 crowns while to Paris it was flat at 7.25.
